rationale: A wins because it treats the launch like raw material, not finished news. Its "A 22% drop in no-shows is the number the fitness industry has been guessing at for years" angle is useful because it immediately attacks the baseline, sample, and self-selection problem; B's "The software behind 50,000 studios wants AI to solve fitness's empty-slot problem" reaches for a tidy trend before it has enough facts. B is competent, but A gives the founder sharper stories and sharper reasons not to pitch them yet.
gaps_in_A: "The company that owns ClassPass now decides which classes fill first" overstates the supplied facts. Mindbody owns ClassPass and has scheduling software; the update does not prove ClassPass inventory or member priority affects the assistant.
"studio front desks stopped having time to do" implies a staffing/workload premise the update does not supply. It needs a named studio or operator evidence before that line earns its attitude.
"a margin and retention play" is plausible PE logic, but it is still inference. The set admits this angle is thin, but the headline should not outrun proof from internal framing or an exec quote.
gaps_in_B: "most boutique studios will never buy an AI tool" is invented context. It may be true, but it is not in the update, and the angle leans on it.
"The prevailing pattern that reporter is tracking is AI as a paid add-on or premium tier" needs proof before it can be a contrarian angle. Right now it is a market thesis stapled to one pricing fact.
"journalist-fit-check — four viable shapes exist" is premature. The first next step is proving the 22% pilot claim, not building lists around a number that may collapse on methodology.

Refusing "Mindbody's assistant sets up a conflict with its own ClassPass marketplace" as pure hallucination throws away the sharpest structural question. The conflict is not proven, but the ownership-and-allocation angle is real if framed as a question, not an accusation.
